growth_story.headline: Puerto Rico's income per person grew briskly until 2004, then stalled for two decades of emigration and bankruptcy before passing its old high in 2024.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Puerto Rico grew 3.1 percent a year from 1990 to 2004, while a federal tax credit drew firms with patents, above all drug makers, to the island. The credit was phased out by 2006, and from 2005 to 2025 growth averaged just 0.1 percent a year. Over 2006–2015 income per person shrank 0.2 percent a year, investment fell from 19.8 percent of GDP in 1999 to 8.0 in 2016, and many people left the island. The government filed for bankruptcy in May 2017, the year Hurricane Maria struck, and income per person fell 0.9 percent in both 2017 and 2018 and 3.6 percent in 2020. Growth then picked up, with 4.3 percent in 2022 and 3.2 in 2024, for an average of 0.7 percent a year over 2016–2025. In 2024 income per person passed its 2004 high for the first time.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe deep crisis: bankruptcy, a destructive hurricane and two decades of large emigration. Yet in the data, income per person fell only slowly, by 0.2 percent a year over 2006–2015, and reached a new peak in 2025. Part of the gap may be arithmetic: when many people leave, output is shared among fewer residents, so income per person can hold up better than the economy as a whole.
